/bin/bash -c "mkdir -p tmp/pdfs && python3 - <<'PY'
from pypdf import PdfReader
from pathlib import Path
r=PdfReader('manuscript.pdf')
print('PAGES:',len(r.pages))
print('METADATA:',r.metadata)
pages=[]
for i,p in enumerate(r.pages,1):
    t=p.extract_text()
    pages.append(f'\\n===== PAGE {i} =====\\n{t}\\n')
Path('tmp/pdfs/manuscript.txt').write_text(''.join(pages))
print(''.join(pages[:3]))
PY"

strengths: The mean-point correspondence is a simple, original, and practically useful way to address the difficult four-point, three-view pose problem using established five-point and P3P solvers. The contribution lies in the approximation and its effective integration with robust estimation; it does not require a new exact algebraic solver to have value.

The reported results demonstrate useful accuracy and efficiency options. In Table 2, the fully enhanced mean-point-plus-offset solver achieves AUC@10 of 77.14 versus 73.53 for homotopy continuation on PhotoTourism. The simpler mean-point solver with refinement, filtering, and ENM nearly matches the enhanced five-point baseline's accuracy (76.16 versus 76.20), while reducing runtime from 56.52 to 44.51 ms.

Evaluation is extensive: 90,000 triplets across 18 scenes and three datasets, with both PoseLib and GC-RANSAC. The supplement examines noise, outliers, scene geometry, thresholds, individual scenes, and an alternative metric covering all three camera pairs. Ablations identify the importance of refinement and ENM, while parameter selection uses a held-out validation scene.

The manuscript clearly acknowledges that the solvers are approximate and explains why the virtual correspondence supplies an additional perspective constraint. Source-code and archived data links, together with implementation settings and hardware descriptions, support reproducibility. These strengths provide a stronger case for acceptance than the reservations below provide for rejection.
weaknesses: Runtime comparisons with homotopy continuation are confounded by initialization. Section 8.3, footnote 8, reports approximately 45 ms for loading weights and other data once per RANSAC invocation; Table 2 reports total HC runtimes of roughly 60–67 ms. Reusing this data across triplets could materially change the comparison. The manuscript does not establish the runtime advantage under amortized initialization, although this concern does not invalidate the accuracy improvements.

The claim of the best speed–accuracy trade-off is incompletely established against the strongest five-point baseline. Figure 4 includes five-point variants with and without ENM, but omits the additional refinement/filtering variants reported in Table 2. Against the fully enhanced baseline, the highest-accuracy proposed variant gains 0.94 AUC@10 percentage points on PhotoTourism while taking 112.60 rather than 56.52 ms. The table supports a useful trade-off, but does not establish superiority at matched runtime.

The geometric bound provides limited control over estimator accuracy. Lemma 1 bounds virtual-point epipolar error by the triangle's spatial extent, which can be large; it does not bound rotation/translation error or guarantee refinement convergence. Figure 9 also shows approximation bias with noiseless observations. Thus, the empirical justification as a RANSAC initializer is stronger than the broad claim that ENM makes scene dependence negligible.

There are smaller reporting and reproducibility issues. The exact refinement residuals, gauge handling, and conversion from the affine fundamental matrix to perspective camera poses are not fully specified. Table 7 also contains identical Cambridge results across all reported columns for the affine and mean-point variants with +R+F, and again with +R+F+ENM; these entries warrant verification. These are secondary concerns rather than reasons to reject the central contribution.
